label: thm2_extend
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm2_extend}
For every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ there exists $K:=K(\varepsilon)>0$ such that the following holds. Let $G$ be an infinite, connected, locally finite graph such that for all vertices $v\in V$,
\[
\mathbb{P}^X_v(\forall t \geq 1: X_t\neq v)\geq \varepsilon.
\]
Then $\kappa^{\mathrm{site}}(G) \leq K< \infty$.
head: environment

label: gapat1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{gapat1}
There exists a universal constant $\varepsilon_1>0$ such that $p_c=1$ or $p_c\leq 1-\varepsilon_1$ for any infinite, connected, locally finite, vertex-transitive graph $G$.
head: environment
name: Gap at 1 for site percolation on vertex transitive graphs

label: dim2
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{dim2}
Let $G$ be an infinite, connected, locally finite graph with conductances $c$ as in \eqref{conductances}. Then
\[
\mathrm{Dim}(G;c)>2 \implies \kappa^{\mathrm{site}}(G) < \infty.
\]
In particular, if there exist $\beta > 0$ and $d>2$ such that $|\partial^E K|_c \geq \beta |K|_\pi^{(d-1)/d}$ for all finite $K\subset V$, then there exists $M:=M(\beta,d)$ such that $\kappa^{\mathrm{site}}(G) \leq M < \infty$.
head: environment

label: first_bound_pres
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{first_bound_pres}
Let $\Pi$ be a minimal vertex cutset separating a vertex $o$ from $\infty$, and let $A$ be the connected component of $o$ in $G \setminus \Pi$. Then
$$\partial^VA = \Pi.$$
Moreover, for every $\pi \in \Pi$ there exists a ray $(v_0, v_1, \ldots)$, with $v_0 = \pi$, such that
$$v_j \notin A \cup \Pi \qquad \forall j \geq 1.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $v \in \partial^VA \setminus \Pi$, then $v$ is present in $G \setminus \Pi$ and adjacent to $A$, contradicting that $A$ is a connected component. Hence $\partial^VA \subseteq \Pi$.

Now fix $\pi \in \Pi$. By minimality, the component of $o$ in $G \setminus (\Pi \setminus \{\pi\})$ is infinite and therefore contains a ray from $o$. This ray avoids $\Pi \setminus \{\pi\}$ and, since $A$ is finite, must leave $A$ through $\pi$. Thus $\pi \in \partial^VA$, proving the remaining inclusion and thus that $\partial^VA = \Pi$.

Take the tail of the ray, beginning at the first visit to $\pi$. It avoids $\Pi \setminus \{\pi\}$. If it entered $A$ after its first visit to $\pi$, then, because $A$ is finite and vertices in a ray are not repeated, it would later have to leave $A$ through $\Pi \setminus \{\pi\}$. This is impossible.
head: environment

label: second_bound_pres
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The hypotheses and Lemma~\ref{first_bound_pres} give
$$\Pi \subseteq \partial^VS \subseteq A \cup \Pi.$$
Indeed, every $\pi \in \Pi$ has a neighbour in $S$ and $\pi \notin A \supset S$, giving the first inclusion. Moreover, if $v\notin S$ but $v\sim u$ for some $u \in S$ then either $v\in A$, or $v\notin A$ and since $u\in A$ also, $v\in \partial^VA = \Pi$ by Lemma~\ref{first_bound_pres}.

Now, fix $\pi \in \Pi$ and use the ray supplied by Lemma~\ref{first_bound_pres}. It avoids $A \cup (\Pi \setminus \{\pi\})$, hence avoids $S \cup (\partial^VS \setminus \{\pi\})$. Therefore $\pi \in \partial_\infty^V S$.

Conversely, let $v \in \partial^VS \setminus \Pi$ (this is enough, since $\partial_\infty^V S \subset \partial^V S$). Then $v \in A$. Every path from $v$ to infinity must leave $A$ through $\Pi$, but $\Pi \subseteq \partial^VS \setminus \{v\}$ so there cannot exist a path from $v$ to $\infty$ in $G\setminus (S\cup (\partial^VS\setminus \{v\}))$. Hence, by definition, $v \notin \partial_\infty^V S$.
head: environment

label: markov
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Markov property of the GFF

label: strong_markov
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{strong_markov}
Let $G$ and $\varphi$ be as in Lemma~\ref{markov}, and let $\Lambda \subset V$ be a finite, non-empty, possibly random set. Assume also that $\Lambda$ is a stopping set, in the sense that $\{\Lambda = \lambda\} \in \sigma(\varphi (v): v\in \lambda)$ for every finite $\lambda \subset V$. Then \eqref{eq:markov} and \eqref{eq:hK} hold conditionally on $\mathcal{H} = \sigma\big(\Lambda, \{\varphi(v) : v \in \Lambda\}\big)$.
head: environment
name: Strong Markov property of the GFF

label: prop3
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop3}
Let $G'=(V',E')$ be a finite, connected graph. Let $\mathbb{P}$ be a positively associated percolation measure on $G'$. Let $B\subset V'$, let $\theta,p\in(0,1]$ and suppose that $\mathbb{P}(u\leftrightarrow B)\geq \theta$ for every $u\in V'$, and $\mathbb{P}(e \text{ is open})\geq p$ for every $e\in E'$. Then for every $o\in V'$,
\[
\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcap_{b\in B}\{o\leftrightarrow b\}\right) \geq c^{|B|},
\]
where $c:=\left(\dfrac{p\theta}{2}\right)^{3/\theta}$.
head: environment

label: cayley_gap
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cayley_gap}
There is a universal constant $\varepsilon>0$ such that $p_c(G')\leq1-\varepsilon$ for site percolation on any Cayley graph $G'$ of superlinear growth.

label: benj
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{benj}
Let $H\leq\mathrm{Aut}(G)$. Then $p_c(G) \leq p_c(G/H)$ for site percolation.
head: environment

label: groups
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{groups}
Suppose that $H \leq\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ satisfies $|Hv| \leq k$ for some $k \geq 1$ and every $v \in V$. For each $v \in V$ and $p \in [0,1]$, the cluster of $\tau(v)$ in Bernoulli-$(1-(1-p)^k)$ site percolation on $G/H$ stochastically dominates the image under $\tau$ of the cluster of $v$ in Bernoulli-$p$ site percolation on $G$. That is,
\[
\mathbb{P}^{G/H}_{1-(1-p)^k}\!\left(C_{\tau(v)} \in A\right) \geq 
\mathbb{P}^{G}_{p}\!\left(\tau(C_v) \in A\right)
\]
for every increasing measurable set $A \subseteq \{0,1\}^{V/H}$, and where by writing $S\in A$ for some $S\subset V/H$, we mean $\mathbf{1}_S\in A$.

name: A site percolation/vertex-orbit version

title: Proof

label: lp6.41
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{lp6.41}
View $G$ as a network with arbitrary edge conductances and suppose that $|V(G)|_\pi = \infty$. Let $A$ be a finite set of vertices. Suppose also that $\varphi(t) := \varphi(G, A, t)$ has the property that $\varphi(t) \geq f(t)$ for some increasing function $f$ on $[|A|_\pi, \infty)$ that satisfies $0 < f(t) \leq t$ and $f(2t) \leq \alpha f(t)$ for some $\alpha$. Then
\[
\mathscr{R}(A \leftrightarrow \infty) \leq \int_{|A|_\pi}^\infty \frac{4\alpha^2}{f(t)^2} dt.
\]
head: environment

label: harmonic_cover
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{harmonic_cover}
Let $G$ be an infinite, connected, locally finite graph. Assume also that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that for all vertices $v\in V$, $\mathbb{P}^X_v(\forall t \geq 1: X_t\neq v)\geq \varepsilon$. Let $A$ be a finite, connected set in $V(G)$ with vertex boundary $\Pi$. Then, for any vertex $o\in A$, there exists a set $Y\subset A$ containing $o$ such that, for all $v\in A$, $\mathbb{P}^X_v(\mathrm{T}_Y<\mathrm{T}_\Pi)\geq 1/2$ and $|Y|<4|\Pi|/\varepsilon$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We define a sequence of nested sets in the following way. Let $Y_1 := \{o\}$. Having defined $Y_1 \subset Y_2 \subset \cdots \subset Y_i$, define
\[
W_i := \left\{v \in A : \mathbb{P}^X_v(T_{Y_i} < T_\Pi) \geq \frac{1}{2}\right\}.
\]
Note that $W_i$ is non-empty for all $i$ since $o \in Y_i$ implies $o \in W_i$. If $W_i \neq A$, then, since $A$ is connected, there exists an edge $\{u,v\} \in E$ with $u \in W_i$ and $v \notin W_i$; let $Y_{i+1} := Y_i \cup \{v\}$ and $y_{i+1} := v$. Otherwise, if $W_J = A$ for some $J$, take $Y := Y_J$. Note that $J < \infty$ since $A$ is finite.

Consider now the effective conductances
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cond_def}
\mathcal{C}_i := \mathcal{C}(Y_i, \Pi) := \sum_{y \in Y_i} \sum_{z \sim y} c(y,z)\mathbb{P}^X_z(T_\Pi < T_{Y_i}).
\end{equation}
Write $q_i(z) := \mathbb{P}^X_z(T_{Y_i} < T_\Pi)$ and $r_i(z) := \mathbb{P}^X_z(T_{y_{i+1}} < T_{Y_i \cup \Pi})$, so that
\[
q_{i+1}(z) = \mathbb{P}^X_z(T_{Y_{i+1}} < T_\Pi) = q_i(z) + r_i(z)\big(1 - q_i(y_{i+1})\big),
\]
since either $Y_i$ is hit before $\Pi$, or $y_{i+1}$ is hit before $Y_i$ and $\Pi$, and then $\Pi$ is hit before $Y_i$, starting afresh from $y_{i+1}$ and using the strong Markov property. Define also the symmetric bilinear form
\[
\mathcal{E}(f,g) := \sum_{\{x,y\} \in E} c(x,y) \big(f(x) - f(y)\big)\big(g(x)-g(y)\big),
\]
commonly called the \textit{energy}, or \textit{Dirichlet energy}, where the sum is over unordered edges. Write $\mathcal{E}(f) := \mathcal{E}(f,f)$. It is a standard fact (often called the \textit{Dirichlet principle}; see, for example, \cite[Exercise~1.3.11]{doyleRandomWalksElectric2000}) that $\mathcal{E}(q_i) = \mathcal{C}_i$. However, we shall include the proof here due to its brevity and the usefulness of some intermediate expressions:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{E}(f,g)
  &= \frac12 \sum_{x\in V}\sum_{y\sim x} c(x,y)\big(f(x)-f(y)\big)\big(g(x)-g(y)\big) \\
  &= \frac12 \sum_{x\in V}\sum_{y\sim x} c(x,y)\,f(x)\big(g(x)-g(y)\big)
   - \frac12 \sum_{x\in V}\sum_{y\sim x} c(x,y)\,f(y)\big(g(x)-g(y)\big) \\
  &= \sum_{x\in V} f(x) \sum_{y\sim x} c(x,y)\big(g(x)-g(y)\big),
\end{align*}
by noting that the conductances are symmetric and symmetrising the sum over edges. Then since $q_i$ is harmonic off $Y_i \cup \Pi$, equal to $1$ on $Y_i$, and $0$ on $\Pi$, we have that
\[
\mathcal{E}(q_i) = \sum_{x \in Y_i} \sum_{z \sim x} c(x,z)\big(1 - q_i(z)\big) = \mathcal{C}_i,
\]
since for $x\notin Y_i \cup \Pi$, $\sum_{z\sim x}c(x,z)(q_i(x)-q_i(z)) = \pi(x)\,q_i(x) - \sum_{z\sim x} c(x,z)q_i(z)$, and harmonicity gives $q_i(x) = \sum_{z\sim x} \frac{c(x,z)}{\pi(x)}q_i(z)$. Thus,
\[
\mathcal{C}_{i+1} - \mathcal{C}_i = \mathcal{E}\big(q_i + r_i(1-q_i(y_{i+1}))\big) - \mathcal{E}(q_i) = 2\big(1-q_i(y_{i+1})\big)\mathcal{E}(q_i,r_i) + \big(1-q_i(y_{i+1})\big)^2\mathcal{E}(r_i,r_i)
\]
by expanding the quadratic form. Since $q_i$ is harmonic away from $Y_i \cup \Pi$ and $r_i \equiv 0$ on this set, the first term vanishes. Moreover, $r_i$ is harmonic away from $Y_i \cup \Pi \cup \{y_{i+1}\}$ and equals $1$ at $y_{i+1}$, so, by one-step decomposition,
\[
\mathcal{E}(r_i) = \sum_{z \sim y_{i+1}} c(y_{i+1},z)\big(1 - r_i(z)\big) = \mathbb{P}^X_{y_{i+1}}\big(T_{Y_i \cup \Pi} < T_{y_{i+1}}^+\big) \geq \mathbb{P}^X_{y_{i+1}}\big(\forall t \geq 1 : X_t \neq y_{i+1}\big) \geq \varepsilon,
\]
since the walk a.s. leaves any finite set and it must do so through its vertex boundary. Thus
\[
\mathcal{C}_{i+1} - \mathcal{C}_i \geq \big(1 - q_i(y_{i+1})\big)^2 \varepsilon.
\]
Finally, $y_{i+1} \notin Y_i$, so $q_i(y_{i+1}) < \tfrac{1}{2}$, hence
\[
\mathcal{C}_{i+1} - \mathcal{C}_i \geq \frac{\varepsilon}{4}.
\]
On the other hand, by \eqref{eq:cond_def} and symmetry of effective conductance\footnote{This can be seen by writing $\mathcal{C}(\Pi,Y_i) = \mathcal{E}(1-q_i) = \mathcal{E}(q_i) = \mathcal{C}(Y_i,\Pi)$.}, $\mathcal{C}_J \leq |\Pi|$. Also,
\[
\mathcal{C}_1 = \sum_{y \sim o}c(o,y) \mathbb{P}^X_y(T_\Pi < T_o) = \mathbb{P}^X_o(T_\Pi < T_o^+) \geq \varepsilon.
\]
Using the recursion, $\mathcal{C}_J - \mathcal{C}_1 \geq (J-1)\varepsilon/4$, so
\[
|\Pi| \geq \mathcal{C}_J \geq (J-1)\frac{\varepsilon}{4} + \varepsilon = \frac{\varepsilon}{4}(J+3),
\]
whence
\[
J \leq \frac{4|\Pi|}{\varepsilon} - 3 < \frac{4}{\varepsilon}|\Pi|.
\]
head: environment

label: strenthened_assump
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{strenthened_assump}
It is at this exact point that stronger assumptions than those of \cite[Theorem~2]{easoCountingMinimalCutsets2025} become necessary. In the proof sketched in \cite[Section~9]{easoCountingMinimalCutsets2025}, the authors prescribe GFF values on either endpoint of the cutset edges; this makes the harmonic extension on $A$ positive everywhere automatically. The analogous event for a vertex cutset would be the prescription of positive GFF values on all neighbours in $A$ of cutset vertices, which is generally degree dependent. If instead one does not prescribe these values, the harmonic extension in $A$ would be negative near its boundary, causing a future argument (namely, the positivity of $g(\varepsilon)$ in \eqref{eq:sgn_positive}) to fail. As can be seen above, Proposition~\ref{harmonic_cover} side-steps this.
head: environment
